\section[\hi{फिर}]{\hi{फिर} (phir) — \textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} the seed of \textquotedblleft{}see you again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-phir}



\begin{quote}
One small word turns a goodbye from \textquotedblleft{}farewell\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{till next time}.\textquotedblright{} Here it is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{फ}} (\emph{pha}, an aspirated \emph{p} — a puff of breath) + \textbf{\hi{ि}} (the \emph{i}-mātrā, written \emph{before} the consonant but read after) + \textbf{\hi{र}} (\emph{ra}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{फिर}} (\emph{phir}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{फिर}} (\emph{phir}) means \textquotedblleft{}again, then, afterwards.\textquotedblright{} It is a native Indo-Aryan adverb (from Prakrit, ultimately tied to the sense \textquotedblleft{}back, return\textquotedblright{}) with no tidy English cognate — but its \emph{job} is one English shares: it turns a parting into a promise. English \textquotedblleft{}see you \textbf{again},\textquotedblright{} Hindi \emph{phir milenge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet \textbf{again}\textquotedblright{}). The optimism is the same; only the word is Indian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{फ} (\emph{pha}, an aspirated \emph{p}) + \hi{ि} (the \emph{i}-mātrā, written before but read after) + \hi{र} (\emph{ra}) $\to$ \hi{फिर}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}phir\textquotedblright{} — mind the aspirated \emph{ph}
  \item what it adds to a goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}again / then\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{phir} mean, and what does it do to a farewell? (\textquotedblleft{}Again / then\textquotedblright{}; it makes the parting a promise of return.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[milenge]{\hi{मिलेंगे} (milenge) — \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-milenge}



\begin{quote}
Your first future-tense verb — and the other half of \textquotedblleft{}see you again.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{म}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\hi{ि}}$\to$\textbf{\hi{मि}} (\emph{mi}); \textbf{\hi{ल}} (\emph{la}) + \textbf{\hi{े}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{ले}} (\emph{le}); the \emph{anusvāra} \textbf{\hi{ं}} nasalises; \textbf{\hi{गे}} (\emph{ge}). Read \textbf{\hi{मि}·\hi{ले}·\hi{ं}·\hi{गे}} $\to$ \emph{milenge}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}} (\emph{milenge}, \textquotedblleft{}we/they will meet\textquotedblright{}) is the future of the verb \textbf{\hi{मिलना}} (\emph{milnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to meet, to be found, to get\textquotedblright{}), from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{मिल्}} (\emph{mil-}, \textquotedblleft{}to join, unite\textquotedblright{}) — the root behind \emph{milan} (\textquotedblleft{}a union, a meeting\textquotedblright{}), a common word and name. The ending \textbf{-\hi{एंगे}} (\emph{-enge}) is the plural future: \emph{milenge} = \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how Hindi builds the future}]
Hindi marks the future with an ending on the verb stem: \emph{mil-} (\textquotedblleft{}meet\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-enge} (\textquotedblleft{}we/they will\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{milenge}. No helper-word like English \textquotedblleft{}will\textquotedblright{} — the tense lives in the ending, the way Hindi's person lives in \emph{hūṁ/hai/haiṁ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{मि} (\emph{mi}) + \hi{ले} (\emph{le}) + the \emph{anusvāra} + \hi{गे} (\emph{ge}) $\to$ \hi{मिलेंगे} (\emph{milenge}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}milenge\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root and its cousin-noun (\emph{mil-} \textquotedblleft{}to join,\textquotedblright{} \emph{milan} \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{})
  \item how the future is marked (an ending on the stem, not a helper-word)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb is \emph{milenge} from, and how does Hindi show \textquotedblleft{}will\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Milnā} \textquotedblleft{}to meet,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{mil-}; with the ending \emph{-enge}, not a separate word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे}]{\hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे} (phir milenge) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-phir-milenge}



\begin{quote}
The warm, everyday goodbye — the one you actually hear, far more than Chapter 1's formal \emph{alvidā}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे}} = \textbf{\hi{फिर}} (\emph{phir}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}} (\emph{milenge}, \textquotedblleft{}we will meet\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll meet again}.\textquotedblright{} Where Chapter 1's \textbf{\hi{अलविदा}} (\emph{alvidā}) is a grave, final farewell (and, fittingly, a \textbf{Perso-Arabic} word — \emph{al-widā}, \textquotedblleft{}the farewell\textquotedblright{}), \emph{phir milenge} is native, everyday, and hopeful. It is the exact sibling of the \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} goodbyes across South Asia — Tamil, Bengali, Marathi all say \textquotedblleft{}I'll come again\textquotedblright{} rather than \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two registers of goodbye}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{अलविदा}} (\emph{alvidā}) — formal, final, Perso-Arabic; for long or last partings.
  \item \textbf{\hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे}} (\emph{phir milenge}) — everyday, warm, native; \textquotedblleft{}till we meet again.\textquotedblright{} Even more casual: \emph{phir milte haiṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}(we) meet again,\textquotedblright{} present for a near future).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the warm goodbye — \emph{phir milenge}
  \item how it differs from \emph{alvidā} (everyday/hopeful vs. formal/final)
  \item the two words it's built from (\emph{phir} + \emph{milenge})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{phir milenge} literally say, and when would you use it over \emph{alvidā}? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll meet again\textquotedblright{}; for everyday partings, where \emph{alvidā} is formal and final.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं}]{\hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं} (kal milte haiṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-kal-milte-hain}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye for tomorrow — built on a word that means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{क}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\hi{ल}} (\emph{la}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{कल}} (\emph{kal}). Two of the simplest letters, one of the trickiest words.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{कल}} (\emph{kal}) means \textbf{both \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}} — the same word for the day on either side of today. It is from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{काल}} (\emph{kāla}, \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}) — the very root that sits inside Punjabi's \emph{akāl} (\textquotedblleft{}timeless\textquotedblright{}). Hindi trusts context (and the verb's tense) to tell which \emph{kal} you mean: \emph{kal milte haiṁ} (present-ish $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow}\textquotedblright{}), \emph{kal milā} (past $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yesterday}\textquotedblright{}).

\textbf{\hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं}} = \emph{kal} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{milte haiṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}we meet,\textquotedblright{} present used for a near-certain future) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{see you tomorrow}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the present-for-future}]
\emph{milte haiṁ} is literally \textquotedblleft{}(we) meet\textquotedblright{} — Hindi, like English (\textquotedblleft{}I'm seeing you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}), uses the present for a scheduled future. \emph{Milte} (the habitual participle) + \emph{haiṁ} (the \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{} you learned in Chapter 3).
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{क} (\emph{ka}) + \hi{ल} (\emph{la}) $\to$ \hi{कल} (\emph{kal}). Two simple letters, one tricky word.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kal milte haiṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the puzzle — \emph{kal} means both \textbf{tomorrow} and \textbf{yesterday}
  \item the root and its Punjabi cousin (\emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{}; \emph{akāl} \textquotedblleft{}timeless\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two opposite days does \emph{kal} mean, and what tells them apart? (Both tomorrow and yesterday; the sentence's tense/context.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{चलता} \hi{हूँ}]{\hi{चलता} \hi{हूँ} (chaltā hūṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll be off\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-chalta-hun}



\begin{quote}
The casual \textquotedblleft{}I'm heading out\textquotedblright{} — and your first taste of how a Hindi verb changes for a man or a woman speaking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{च}} (\emph{ca}) + \textbf{\hi{ल}} (\emph{la}) + the long-\emph{ā} mātrā $\to$ \textbf{\hi{चलता}} (\emph{caltā}); with \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} (\emph{hūṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am,\textquotedblright{} from Chapter 3). Read \emph{caltā hūṁ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{चलता} \hi{हूँ}} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I go / I move},\textquotedblright{} used the way English says \textquotedblleft{}I'll be off / I'll get going.\textquotedblright{} The verb is \textbf{\hi{चलना}} (\emph{calnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to move, walk, go\textquotedblright{}), from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{चल्}} (\emph{cal-}, \textquotedblleft{}to move, stir\textquotedblright{}) — the root behind \emph{cal} (\textquotedblleft{}move!\textquotedblright{}), \emph{calan} (\textquotedblleft{}circulation\textquotedblright{}), and \emph{cañcal} (\textquotedblleft{}restless\textquotedblright{}). Like Bengali \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{}) and Marathi \emph{yeto}, Hindi prefers to leave by saying \textquotedblleft{}I'm \textbf{moving},\textquotedblright{} never a blunt \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb agrees with the speaker's gender}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a man says \textbf{\hi{चलता} \hi{हूँ}} (\emph{caltā hūṁ})
  \item a woman says \textbf{\hi{चलती} \hi{हूँ}} (\emph{caltī hūṁ})
\end{itemize}

The \emph{-tā / -tī} ending marks the speaker's gender — a feature English has no trace of, and one you will meet again and again. (Compare Marathi \emph{yeto} m. / \emph{yete} f.)
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{च} (\emph{ca}) + \hi{ल} (\emph{la}) + long \emph{ā} $\to$ \hi{चलता} (\emph{caltā}), with \hi{हूँ} (\emph{hūṃ}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY (m.): \emph{caltā hūṁ}  ·  (f.): \emph{caltī hūṁ}{]}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the verb and root (\emph{calnā} \textquotedblleft{}to move,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit \emph{cal-})
  \item \emph{Say it:} why Hindi says \textquotedblleft{}I move\textquotedblright{} and not \textquotedblleft{}I leave\textquotedblright{} (the softer, non-final parting)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{chaltā hūṁ} literally mean, and how does a woman say it? (\textquotedblleft{}I go/move\textquotedblright{} = I'll be off; \emph{caltī hūṁ}, with the feminine \emph{-tī}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:HI-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Four ways to part, from the formal to the offhand.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item formal, final (Perso-Arabic) — \emph{alvidā}
  \item everyday, \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{phir milenge}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kal milte haiṁ}
  \item casual \textquotedblleft{}I'll be off\textquotedblright{} (m./f.) — \emph{caltā hūṁ / caltī hūṁ}
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}(we) will meet\textquotedblright{} (\emph{phir}, \emph{milenge})
  \item the word that means BOTH tomorrow and yesterday (\emph{kal})
  \item the verb behind \textquotedblleft{}I'll be off\textquotedblright{} (\emph{calnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{milenge} $\leftarrow$ \emph{mil-} \textquotedblleft{}to join\textquotedblright{} (\emph{milan}, \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{kal} $\leftarrow$ \emph{kāla} \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} (cousin of Punjabi \emph{akāl}, \textquotedblleft{}timeless\textquotedblright{})
  \item \emph{caltā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{cal-} \textquotedblleft{}to move\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{-tā/-tī} ending marks the speaker's gender
  \item \emph{alvidā} $\leftarrow$ Perso-Arabic \emph{al-widā}, \textquotedblleft{}the farewell\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You're leaving a friend and expect to see them next week. Which goodbye fits, and how would a woman sign off casually? (\emph{Phir milenge}; \emph{caltī hūṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
